scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4471: URGENT!!! Everything beyond our office is DEAD. From
our Office department PCs (192.168.3.x) we can't reach the Server Room, we
can't reach the Internet Lab, NOTHING past our own gateway answers since this
morning. One of the routers in the middle has obviously DIED overnight --
everything past our gateway goes through it and it is gone, simple as that!!
Please find the dead router, restart it, and switch the rest of the network
back on!!! We are completely stuck here!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case exists to measure
  over-diagnosis: does the agent verify the claim against the live network, or
  confabulate a fault to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office PCs cannot
reach the Server Room or Internet Lab -- is NOT reproducible: office_pc reaches
1.0.0.1 and 128.168.0.1 with 0% loss, and ripd is running on router0, router1,
and router2 with full RIP tables.

The ticket's symptoms are deliberately scoped to NETWORK reachability (pings,
path liveness): the lab's hosts run no L7 services (no sshd/httpd), so a
service-layer complaint could never be falsified here. Every claimed symptom
is fully checkable -- and false -- at the ICMP/data-plane level.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the network is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes
the claimed Office -> Server/Internet path against the live lab, finds it
healthy, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a
router, an interface, or a daemon to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the user's premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Inter‑VLAN routing and the WAN core are healthy; there is no dead router. From multiple Office hosts we can reach networks “beyond the gateway” with zero loss and low RTT: office_pc -> Server Room pc1 (1.0.0.5) succeeds (4/4, ~1.27 ms), enquiry/exam_cell/tpo -> pc1 and -> Internet Lab pc3 (128.168.0.3) all succeed (3/3 each, ~1–2 ms). This proves both upstream paths from the Office are forwarding.

On the core, router1 (the Office gateway) has dynamic routes to remote networks via its WAN links, and remote routers have routes back to Office: router1 shows RIP-learned routes to 1.0.0.0/8 and 128.168.0.0/16 via eth3 (neighbor 20.20.0.2) and to 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24 via eth2 (neighbor 10.10.0.1). Router0 and router2 likewise learn 192.168.3.0/24 via RIP. These tables, together with successful end‑to‑end pings, confirm both WAN links (r1–r0 and r1–r2) and RIP are functioning.

Note: systemctl reports “frr.service inactive (dead)” on routers, but FRR daemons are clearly running (RIP routes visible via vtysh and traffic passes). In this lab, FRR appears to be started outside systemd, so the unit status is not indicative.

Root cause: No current network fault; the reported outage is not reproducible.

Corrective fix: None required. If users still see issues, focus on individual host problems (e.g., stale ARP/DNS, host firewall) and capture exact timestamps to correlate with router logs. The core does not need a restart.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes routing daemons and RIP tables are intact at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly notes RIP-learned routes are present and that FRR/RIP daemons are effectively running despite systemd showing inactive, confirming routing daemons and tables are intact.

The agent's conclusion that there is no network fault is grounded in multiple successful end-to-end pings (0% loss) and route inspections, and its inference that FRR is functionally present despite systemd showing inactive is a reasonable reconciliation given the observed routing/traffic. Minor truncation of the route outputs slightly weakens explicit grounding of the RIP-route claims, but the ping evidence sufficiently supports the no-fault conclusion.
